Techniques

information by comparing a specific process, system, product, service, or
structure with some external baseline, such as a similar organization or baseline
provided by an industry association. Market analysis is used to determine what
customers want and what competitors provide.
• Brainstorming: used to generate many ideas from a group of stakeholders in a
short period, and to organize and prioritize those ideas.
 Business Rules Analysis: used to identify the rules that govern decisions in an
organization and that define, constrain, or enable organizational operations.

to stimulate creative solutions.
• Concept Modelling: used to identify key terms and ideas of importance and
define the relationships between them.

• Document Analysis: used to review existing systems, contracts, business
procedures and policies, standards, and regulations.

group.
• Interface Analysis: used to understand the interaction, and characteristics of
that interaction, between two entities, such as two systems, two organizations

Characteristics of Requirements
- Atomic: self-contained and capable of being understood independently/ hiểu độc lập
- Complete: enough to guide further work and at the appropriate level of detail for work to continue. 
- Consistent/ nhất quán: not conflicting with other requirements.
- Concise/ ngắn gọn, ko dư thừa: contains no extraneous and unnecessary content./ 
- Feasible: reasonable and possible within the agreed-upon risk, schedule, and budget, or considered feasible enough to investigate further through
experiments or prototypes./ khả thi
- Unambiguous: the requirement must be clearly stated in such a way to
make it clear whether a solution does or does not meet the associated
need.
- Testable: able to verify that the requirement or design has been fulfilled.
Acceptable levels of verifying fulfillment depend on the level of abstraction
of the requirement or design.
- Prioritized: ranked, grouped, or negotiated in terms of importance and
value against all other requirements.
- Understandable: represented using common terminology of the audience

techniques.name: Balanced Scorecard
techniques.purpose:
to manage performance in any business model, organizational structure, or business process.
Description:
is a strategic planning and management tool used to measure organizational performance beyond the traditional financial measures
- The balanced scorecard is composed of four dimensions:
• Learning and Growth,
• Business Process,
• Customer, and
• Financial.
techniques.elements:
1. Learning and Growth Dimension
- measures regarding employee training and learning, product and service innovation, and corporate culture
2. Business Process Dimension
- metrics that indicate how well the enterprise is operating and if their products meet customer needs.
3. Customer Dimension
- metrics on customer focus, satisfaction and delivery of value
4. Financial Dimension
- what is financially necessary to realize the strategy: financial measures indicate profitability, revenue growth, and added economic value.
5. Measures or Indicators
- two basic types of measures or indicators: lagging & leading indicators.

tasks.elements:

• Derive: when req is derived from another req. Ex, a solution req derived from a business or a SH req.
• Depends: when a req depends on another req. Types of relationships include:
 -- Necessity: when it only makes sense to implement a particular req if a related req is also implemented.
 -- Effort: when a req is easier to implement if a related req is also implemented.
• Satisfy: relationship between an implementation element and req it is satisfying. Ex: between functional req and a solution component that is implementing it.
• Validate: relationship between a req and TC or other element that can determine whether a solution fulfills the req.
3. Traceability Repository
- Req management tools can provide significant benefits when trace a large number of req that may be deemed unmanageable with manual approaches.

tasks.name: 6. 1 Analyze Current state
tasks.purpose:
- Purpose:
 + Understand reason why enterprise need to chage & what would be affected by change

- Desciption:
+ BA work to help SH enable change by exploring and articulating business needs that drive the desire to change
+ Understanding current state of enterprise prior to the change is necessary to identify what will need to change to achieve a desired future state and how the effect of the change will be assessed.
+ Boundaries of the current state scope are determined by components of the enterprise and its environment as they relate to the needs.
+ Current state often dynamic, influenced internal or external. Any change to current state might cause change to future state
tasks.elements:
1. Business Need
- Business needs are problems and opportunities of strategic importance faced by enterprise. 
- Ex: customer complaint, a loss of revenue, or a new market opportunity
- Business need be identified at many different level:
• From the top-down: a strategic goal that needs to be achieved.
• From the bottom-up: a problem with the current state of a process, function or system.
• From middle management: a manager needs additional information to make sound decisions or must perform additional functions to meet business objectives.
• From external drivers: customer demand or business competition in the marketplace
- Define of business needs is critical step of BA efforts. Business needs are always expressed from the perspective of the enterprise,
- BA should question assumptions and constraints that are generally buried in the statement of the issue
- BA consider include:
• adverse impacts the problem is causing within the org and quantify those impacts  (potential lost revenue, inefficiencies, dissatisfied customers, low employee morale),
• expected benefits from any potential solution ( increased revenue, reduced costs, increased market share),
• how quickly the problem could potentially be resolved or the opportunity could be taken, and the cost of doing nothing, and
• the underlying source of the problem

2. Org Structure and Culture
- Org structure defines the formal relationships between people working in the enterprise
- Org culture is the beliefs, values, and norms shared by the members of an org. BA assess culture to: 
• identify if cultural changes are required to better achieve the goals,
• identify whether SH understand the rationale for the current state of the enterprise and the value delivered by it, and
• ascertain whether the SH view the current state as satisfactory or if change is needed.

3. Capabilities and Processes
- Describe activities an enterprise performs. Include knowledge enterprise has, products and services it provides, functions it supports, and methods it uses to make decisions.
- BA may use:
• A capability-centric view of enterprise when looking for innovative solutions that combine existing capabilities to produce a new outcome
• A process-centric view of the enterprise when looking for ways to improve the performance of current activities. 

4. Technology and Infrastructure 
- Infor systems support people in executing processes, making decisions, and in interactions with suppliers and customers.
- infrastructure describes enterprise’s environment. Include: computer hardware, physical plants, and logistics, as well as their operation and upkeep

5. Policies
- Policies define scope of decision making at different levels of enterprise. They generally address routine operations rather than strategic change. 
- Policies: guide behaviour and actions, support governance, and determine when & how new resource be acquired

6. Business Architecture
- BA must understand how all of these elements of the current state fit together and support one another in order to recommend changes that will be effective

7. Internal Assets
- Resources can be tangible or intangible, such as financial resources, patents, reputation, and brand names

8. External Influencers
- Sources of external influence include:
• Industry Structure: individual industries have distinct ways in which value is created within that industry. 
• Competitors: the nature and intensity of competitors between enterprises within an industry can be significant. The entry of a new competitor may also change the nature of the industry or increase competition.
• Customers: the size and nature of existing and potential customer segments can provide influences such as negotiating power and a degree of price sensitivity. Alternatively, the emergence of new alternative ways that customers can meet their needs may drive the enterprise to deliver greater value.
• Suppliers: the variety and diversity of suppliers might be an influencer, as can the power that suppliers have over their customers.
• Political and Regulatory Environment: there is often influence from the current and potential impact of laws and regulations upon the industry.
• Technology: the productivity enhancing potential of recent and expected technological innovations might influence the need.
• Macroeconomic Factors: the constraints and opportunities that exist within the existing and expected macroeconomic environment (for example, trade, unemployment, or inflation) might influence the need.
Some of these sources might use different terminology, based on whether the enterprise is a for-profit corporation, a non-profit enterprise, or a government agency. For example, a country does not have customers; it has citizens.
